topic: Feinstein, Adolphs & Damasio (2011/2013): Patient S.M. — Fearless to Snakes & Haunted Houses Until One Breath of 35% CO2
visual_mode_reason: Combines the iconic University of Iowa exotic-pet-store snake/tarantula encounter, Waverly Hills Haunted House, and 35% CO2 inhalation mask test with a 3D Brain cutaway contrasting bilateral amygdala calcification against brainstem chemoreceptor panic circuits.

primary_case.place: Department of Neurology, University of Iowa Carver College of Medicine
primary_case.summary: Justin Feinstein, Ralph Adolphs, Antonio Damasio, and Daniel Tranel (Current Biology 2011; Nature Neuroscience 2013) studied Patient S.M., a 44-year-old woman with complete bilateral amygdala destruction from Urbach-Wiethe disease who showed 0 out of 10 fear toward live snakes, tarantulas, and haunted-house monsters — until a single breath of 35% CO2 triggered her first panic attack in decades!

people.role: University of Iowa & Caltech lesion neuroscientists (Current Biology 2011; Nature Neuroscience 2013)
people.bio: Tested Patient S.M. across snakes, spiders, horror films, and 35% CO2 inhalation, proving the amygdala is required for external threat fear but NOT for interoceptive CO2 suffocation panic.

debate_ignition.prebunk_myth: People believe the amygdala is the single master switch for every kind of fear and panic in the human brain.
debate_ignition.open_verdict_question: If you had to choose, would you rather lose external fear of snakes and monsters or lose internal panic when air runs short?
debate_ignition.offcenter_creator_bet: My bet: external fear is a lifesaver — Patient S.M. proved internal CO2 panic still hits 100% without an amygdala. Keep external fear or erase it?

core_facts.fact: In Feinstein, Adolphs, Damasio & Tranel (2011 Current Biology), Patient S.M. — whose bilateral amygdalae were completely calcified by Urbach-Wiethe disease — rated her fear at 0 out of 10 while holding a live snake for 3 minutes, walking through Waverly Hills Haunted House, and watching 10 horror film clips.

Across 3 months of computerized ecological momentary diary entries (272 random prompts) and 8 standardized fear questionnaires, Patient S.M. reported zero instances of real-world fear despite experiencing normal joy, sadness, anger, and disgust.

At Waverly Hills Sanatorium Haunted House, S.M. walked at the front of the group of 5 women, never hesitated around dark corners, laughed and poked a costumed monster in the head — startling the actor instead of feeling afraid.

In Feinstein et al. (2013 Nature Neuroscience), inhaling a single vital-capacity breath of 35 percent carbon dioxide (CO2) triggered immediate, full-blown panic attacks in 3 out of 3 bilateral amygdala lesion patients (100 percent) compared with only 3 out of 12 healthy controls (25 percent).

Within 8 to 15 seconds of inhaling 35 percent CO2, Patient S.M.'s visual-analog fear and panic scores jumped from 0 to 9.5 out of 10 as she gasped for air and tore at the breathing mask, calling it the first fear she had felt since childhood.

Adolphs et al. (2005 Nature) proved with eye-tracking that S.M.'s deficit in recognizing fearful facial expressions stems from failing to direct gaze naturally to the widened whites of the eyes unless explicitly instructed.

Tovote, Fadok & Lüthi (2015 Nature Reviews Neuroscience) showed that while visual and auditory threats require the basolateral and central amygdala, internal blood-acidification (CO2/H+) activates brainstem retrotrapezoid/parabrachial chemoreceptors and the insula directly.

Because intact amygdala circuitry normally inhibits or regulates downstream brainstem panic generators during mild interoceptive challenges, bilateral amygdala loss left S.M. hyper-vulnerable (100 percent vs 25 percent) to CO2 suffocation panic.
